episode_appearances.video_title: Boost Oxygen — ABC official episode roster
episode_appearances.pitch: Portable supplemental canned oxygen for recreational and non-medical use.
episode_appearances.offer: Kevin O’Leary offered a $1,000,000 loan at 9% interest plus 7.5% equity; the televised final deal was reported as a $1,000,000 loan at 7.5% interest plus 6.25% equity. Rob Neuner and Mike Grice accepted Kevin O’Leary’s revised offer.

timeline.event: ABC aired Boost Oxygen in Season 11, Episode 2; the founders accepted O’Leary’s televised financing/equity offer.
Connecticut Post reported Neuner saying O’Leary had done due diligence and would receive a 5% stake, conflicting with the televised 6.25%.
Florida registered BOOST OXYGEN LLC as a Connecticut foreign LLC, document M20000001997.
O’Leary directly described Boost Oxygen as a company he invested in.
BOOST OXYGEN LLC filed its 2026 Florida annual report and remained ACTIVE in the Florida record.
The official company site offered priced products and continued to describe its O’Leary relationship.

registry_records.jurisdiction: Florida foreign registration / Connecticut home jurisdiction
registry_records.status: active foreign LLC; Connecticut home-state standing unresolved
registry_records.limitation: Florida confirms a Connecticut LLC, FEI/EIN 36-4617519. Connecticut’s search page rendered only Loading/CSS Error in this environment.

claims.text: Boost Oxygen is operating; Kevin O’Leary’s investment is directly corroborated, but contemporaneous sources conflict over the final equity terms.
O’Leary’s own 2020 interview is direct post-show evidence that an investment occurred.
The 6.25% televised figure versus the founder-reported 5% may reflect renegotiated closing terms, but that explanation remains inference without executed documents.

Current company copy reduces the transaction to a 'million-dollar deal' and omits dated loan/equity detail; without an archived version of that same page, this shows narrative simplification but not a proven edit.

episode_appearances.video_title: Boot Illusion pitch — ABC official Shark Tank YouTube
episode_appearances.pitch: Fashion boots with interchangeable uppers and shoe bases.
episode_appearances.offer: Daymond John reportedly offered $100,000 for 75%; Barbara Corcoran offered $100,000 for 55%. Queenie Davis and Andrew Goodrum accepted Barbara Corcoran’s $100,000 for 55% offer.

timeline.event: Boot Illusion aired in Season 3, Episode 13 and accepted Barbara’s $100,000 for 55% offer.
A founder interview reported that the Barbara deal did not proceed and described manufacturing failure, customs delays and order refunds.
BOOT ILLUSION trademark application serial 86028331 was filed to Gwennette Davis for shoe accessories.
Later follow-up reporting says the planned relaunch failed and the business shuttered; no primary filing fixed the exact date.

registry_records.limitation: NY DOS endpoint returned 502. No entity filing tying a corporation/LLC to Boot Illusion was captured.

claims.text: Boot Illusion appears to have closed after its Barbara Corcoran deal did not proceed, but the tracker withholds a definitive closure status because no primary entity filing or exact shutdown record was captured.
Barbara’s deal did not close; evidence is a post-show founder interview rather than an executed termination document.

ABC’s current page links Boot Illusion to Queen Grace Shoes; without archived contemporaneous ABC copy or entity records, this is not treated as proof Queen Grace was the original legal entity or a successor.

episode_appearances.offer: Kendra Scott offered $500,000 for 10%; Barbara Corcoran sought 20% and briefly discussed a joint offer; Kevin O’Leary offered $500,000 for 15%. Ellyette Gheno accepted Kendra Scott’s solo $500,000 for 10% offer.

timeline.event: Gheno founded BootayBag with $300, initially in Denver, according to her 2021 interview.
BootayBag aired in Season 12, Episode 2; Gheno accepted Kendra Scott’s $500,000 for 10% offer.
Bizwomen/San Francisco Business Times reported 40,000 subscribers and manufacturing changes made with Scott’s investment.
Florida formed BOOTAYBAG, LLC, document L24000231706, with Ellyette Gheno as registered agent and authorized member.
BootayBag stopped shipping, deactivated social accounts and shut its website; later founder statements said she chose to close/leave the company.
Inc. reported customer claims of continued charges, missing shipments and lack of closure notice. Those customer claims are allegations, not adjudicated findings.
Gheno wrote that she had exited BootayBag the prior year after building it from $300 to more than $32 million in sales.
Florida administratively dissolved BOOTAYBAG, LLC for failure to file an annual report.
The current domain stated that it no longer delivered products directly and instead linked visitors to similar products on Amazon.

registry_records.limitation: Florida record is definitive only for the 2024 LLC. Trademark history shows BOOTAYBAG CORP. as later mark owner and BootayBag LLC in Denver as original owner; conversion/assignment/merger documents were not captured.

claims.text: BootayBag closed in December 2024; Kendra Scott’s investment is strongly corroborated, while the BootayBag LLC/BOOTAYBAG CORP. succession and any post-closure asset transfer remain unresolved.
Closure is established independently from the later Florida administrative dissolution; the dissolution is not being used as proof the brand failed.
Customer claims about continued charges and missing orders around shutdown are allegations reported by Inc., not adjudicated findings.
Trademark records indicate a transition from BootayBag LLC to BOOTAYBAG CORP., but the exact legal instrument and any post-closure asset sale remain unresolved.

The founder’s public narrative evolved from an initially unclear departure to explicit later discussion of leaving/closing; this is a documented narrative change, not proof that a specific webpage was secretly edited.

The current thebootaybags.com page is an affiliate-oriented domain revival, not evidence that BootayBag resumed direct fulfillment: the page itself says it no longer delivers products directly and routes users to Amazon.

episode_appearances.video_title: Booty Queen — ABC official appearance index
episode_appearances.pitch: Women’s fitness apparel designed around glute-focused training.
episode_appearances.offer: Daymond John offered $250,000 for 33.3%; the founders countered at 25% and 27.5%, but Daymond held to equal one-third ownership. Amanda Latona Kuclo and Steve Kuclo accepted Daymond John’s $250,000 for 33.3% offer.

timeline.event: Trademark-derived records list first use of BOOTYQUEEN in commerce by Bootyqueen Apparel LLC.
Booty Queen Apparel aired on Shark Tank; Amanda and Steve accepted Daymond John’s $250,000 for 33.3% offer.
BOOTYQUEEN registration 5495598 issued to Bootyqueen Apparel LLC.
Follow-up reporting says the company opened a retail store in Plano, Texas.
Daymond John published a verified-channel video saying he invested in Booty Queen Apparel.
Founder LinkedIn histories, as later reported by Shark Tank Blog, indicate shutdown around April 2021; this date was not independently captured from a registry filing.
Later reporting says the company’s social channels ceased updates around mid-2021.
No active primary ecommerce channel or verified successor was located; a registered trademark is treated as IP evidence, not operating evidence.

registry_records.limitation: Trademark-derived records identify Bootyqueen Apparel LLC as a Texas LLC with a Dallas address. Texas’s search portal loaded, but no entity-specific status record was captured in this environment.

claims.text: Booty Queen appears to have stopped operating around 2021, while Daymond John directly confirms that he invested; the tracker withholds a definitive closure status until the Texas entity standing or another primary shutdown record is captured.
Daymond John’s verified-channel statement is direct post-show investor evidence that the relationship went beyond an on-air handshake.
Closure is supported by later-reported founder employment histories plus prolonged inactive commerce/social channels, but the exact legal cessation date is unresolved.
The BOOTYQUEEN mark remains listed as registered in a current USPTO-derived source; that status is intentionally not treated as proof of business operation.
